newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Poet to meet intellectual when Havel visits Brazil.
newsitem.headline: Poet to meet intellectual when Havel visits Brazil.

text.p: A poet-leader will meet an intellectual turned head of government when the president of the Czech Republic, Vaclav Havel, arrives in Brazil on Sunday.

Czech and Brazilian officials said Havel's week-long tour of Latin America's largest country, followed by another week visiting Chile, Argentina and Uruguay, was designed to spur bilateral trade and investment.

But they predicted the personal similarities between Havel and Brazil's President Fernando Henrique Cardoso, along with an emphasis on noncommercial engagements in the Czech president's itinerary, would steal the show.

"President Cardoso is a great intellectual. President Havel is a great writer. They will have a lot to talk about," Marcelo Jardim, director-general of the Brazilian Foreign Ministry's Europe Department, said.

Havel is a poet who played a key role in the former Czechoslovakia's "Velvet Revolution" in 1989, which ended communist rule. Cardoso was a left-wing sociologist when he went into exile under Brazil's 1964-85 military regime.
The two will hold talks on Monday.

Although travelling with the president of his country's central bank and its minister of industry and commerce, Havel has a schedule full of cultural and offbeat engagements. On the first-ever visit by a Czech president to Latin America, he was to travel on Tuesday to the Amazon rain forest, where he will visit the Waimiri-Atroari Indian tribe's jungle reserve.

On Sept. 21 Havel will visit the city of Lidice in the interior of Rio de Janeiro state, named after a Czech town destroyed by the Nazis in the Second World War in retaliation for a Czech partisan attack on a German general.

But Czech Ambassador to Brasilia Antonin Blazek said economics would not be forgotten. In 1995 Brazil exported only $26 million in goods to the Czech Republic, mainly coffee and shoes, and imported $55.4 million, mostly machinery and condensed milk.

Blazek told reporters Czech industrial concern Skoda Praha was considerng building a truck factory in Brazil and Czech firms were interested in irrigation projects, modernisation of Brazil's railways and provision of turbines for power plants.
Between 30 and 40 Czech businessmen were expected to accompany Havel.
